title: The Shipping Lanes Nobody Talks About
standfirst: Most of what we buy passes through a handful of narrow straits.

readingList.title: Choke Points: The Narrow Seas That Run the World
Insurance Costs and Conflict at Sea
What the Energy Crunch Means for Winter Bills

body: Look at the label on almost anything in your house and it probably crossed an ocean to reach you. What few people realise is how much of that trade squeezes through a small number of narrow passages, any one of which can be closed by war, piracy or accident.

The Strait of Malacca links the Indian Ocean to the Pacific and carries a large share of the trade between Asia and Europe. The Suez Canal and the Bab el-Mandeb strait form the short route from Asia to the Mediterranean. The Strait of Hormuz carries much of the world’s seaborne oil. The Panama Canal joins the Atlantic and the Pacific.

Each of these is a single point of failure. When a large container ship ran aground in the Suez Canal in 2021, it held up hundreds of vessels for days and sent ripples through supply chains for weeks.
## What happens when a route closes

Ships can go the long way round, but it costs time and fuel. Rerouting from Suez around the Cape of Good Hope adds well over a week to a voyage between Asia and northern Europe. Insurance costs rise. Some goods arrive late, and some prices climb.

Britain is an island that imports much of its food and energy. Disruption at sea is not a distant problem. It shows up in the price of fuel, in empty shelves and in the cost of goods in the shops. The narrow seas are a long way away, but their effects are felt in every high street.
